endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Reporting Obligations: Recipient must notify the covered entity of any misuse or unauthorized disclosure.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Review incident response plans for alignment with relevant breach reporting, data protection, data privacy, or other laws.

endorsements.title: The EU AI Act: implications and compliance guidance for healthcare facilities
endorsements.quote: The oncology center establishes a direct reporting channel with the vendor for critical incidents and performance anomalies, ensuring the vendor is promptly informed of issues affecting the AI system in real-world clinical use, aiding in their own post-market surveillance.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether contractual incident-notification clauses shorten vendor disclosure time or reduce patient or data harm, and no study in this map documents the harm from delayed disclosure. Three sources endorse the practice, one as a requirement and two as recommendations, so support rests on expert agreement rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, this places the recommendation at no direct evidence. The three endorsements come from two frameworks and one commentary, and none reports data on notification timing or downstream harm.

The CHAI playbook states that a recipient must notify the covered entity of misuse or unauthorized disclosure. NIST AI 600-1 advises reviewing incident response plans for alignment with breach reporting and privacy laws. An EU AI Act commentary describes a direct vendor reporting channel that supports post-market surveillance. None of these sources specifies a notification timeframe.

No study in this map measures how long vendors take to disclose AI safety incidents or what harm accrues during that delay. Without such data, the size of the hazard and the extent to which a contract clause would stop harm before it reaches patients remain unknown.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare the time from incident detection to organizational notification, and the resulting patient or data harm, between vendor contracts with and without defined notification windows. Descriptive audits of existing AI vendor contracts and incident logs would help establish how often delayed disclosure occurs and how long it lasts.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether organizations serving these populations can secure and enforce such clauses, and whether doing so affects harm to their patients, has not been examined.
